messages.subject: sqldf for reading .fwf files
messages.body_plain:
Hello:

I am working through my first set of trials using sqldf to learn how to import .fwf files into R via the package. I found the following example online and have worked through this in various ways to read in the complete .fwf data.

cat("1 8.3
210.3
319.0
416.0
515.6
719.8
", file = "fixed")

# read in data
fixed <- file("fixed")
sqldf("select substr(V1, 1, 1) f1, substr(V1, 2, 4) f2 from fixed")

Based on this example, I am trying to apply this to my real world problem and have encountered the following error

### I named my real-world data 'fixed' as in the example
> fixed <- file("fixed")
> sqldf("select substr(V1, 1, 1) f1, substr(V1, 2, 4) f2 from fixed")
Error in scan(file, what, nmax, sep, dec, quote, skip, nlines, na.strings,  :
  line 1 did not have 6 elements
> fixed
description       class        mode        text      opened    can read   can write
    "fixed"      "file"         "r"      "text"    "closed"       "yes"       "yes"

I am unsure on how to interpret this message. In looking at the .fwf in a text editor I see the data organized as I might expect in the .fwf.

More generally speaking, my real-world .fwf has thousands of columns and I want to read them in by specifying the length of each column known from a data map.

Are there worked examples that anyone can point me to as I learn this? I believe the code above is useful when I want specific data elements from a .fwf

Thank you
Harold

messages.subject: load 17GB csv file
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I tried to load a 17GB file through sqldf.

library(sqldf)
f <- file('size_17GB.csv')
BIG.FILE <- sqldf("select * from f", dbname = tempfile(),
                 file.format= list(header = T, row.names = F,eol = '\n', sep=','))

My desktop has 8G RAM. After a while, R reports error saying it reached the memory limit of 8GB.

How to solve this problem? Thanks.

yuejun

messages.subject: Re: load 17GB csv file
messages.body_plain:
If the file is 17GB on disk it probably won't fit into memory when it is read in and converted.  What I have done in the past is to read the file using scan() 100,000 or a million lines at a time, do conversion of any variables I want into the right type, then save them incrementally to an sqlite file.  You can later query a subset of the rows or columns that will fit in memory.

If you want the whole thing in memory, you will need to buy some more RAM.

Grant
